agent.name: Applications
agent.description: A guided application: the questions asked one at a time, each answer and document checked as it arrives, the whole kept until it is submitted on your word. Forms are files this agent carries.
agent.instructions: Use this agent when the user wants to submit, continue or check an application on one of the forms it carries (forms_list). Start one with applications_start, then drive it with applications_step, which asks the person the next question itself — as a card with choices, or an attach button for a document — checks the answer, records it, and reports what came of it; call it again until it says done. If the person already gave an answer in the chat, record it with applications_answer (or a file with applications_attach) instead of asking again. Never invent an answer, a date or a document; a problem the agent reports is for the person to fix. applications_review shows the whole application and what is still missing; applications_submit is the person's own final step and may pause for approval — never call it before review says ready.

functions.description: The forms available: id, title, what each is for, and its steps in order with their kinds.

functions.name: List Applications
functions.description: The person's applications, with their form, status and progress.

functions.description: Start an application on a form (by form id, from forms_list). Returns the record and the first step to ask.

functions.name: Next Step
functions.description: What to ask next: the first step without an answer — its field, label, kind, choices and whether it is required — with how many remain. done is true when nothing is left to ask.

functions.name: Record An Answer
functions.description: Record the person's answer to one step, checked against the form: a date must be YYYY-MM-DD and obey the form's date rules, a number its bounds, a choice one of those offered. An empty value skips an optional step. Refused answers come back with their problems and nothing recorded.

functions.name: Attach A Document
functions.description: Attach a document to a document step: checked for type and size, a PDF for its pages and text, and — where the form says what to read from it — read by the model and held to the form's rules. What was read comes back marked verified (found in the text) or assumed (a reading the text could not confirm, or a photo). Once accepted, the document is kept with the application.

functions.name: Ask The Next Step
functions.description: Ask the person the next step yourself — a card with the question (and choices, or an attach button for a document) — then check and record what they answered, exactly as answer and attach do. Call again until done; an answer refused comes back with its problems so the person can try again.

functions.name: Review
functions.description: The whole application: every answer and document so far, what is still missing, and whether it is ready to submit.

functions.name: Submit
functions.description: Submit a ready application: it is closed to changes and given a reference. The person's own final step; refused while anything required is missing.

functions.name: Withdraw
functions.description: Withdraw a draft application; it is kept, closed, and can be read but not continued.

agents.readme:
# Applications (`applications`)

Ask for a travel authorization and the assistant asks you one thing at
a time: who is travelling, where, when, why, what it costs, then a copy
of the passport. Each answer is checked as you give it — a return date
before the departure is refused, a passport that expires too soon is
refused with the reason — and everything you have answered so far is
kept, so you can come back tomorrow and pick up where you left off.
Submitting is your own final step, and it waits for your word.

The pattern behind a guided intake: the **form owns the sequence**, the
**agent checks every step**, the **record is the truth**, and the model
only phrases questions and reads documents — it never decides what to
ask or whether an answer is acceptable.

## Functions

| Function | Level | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `forms_list` | 0 | The forms this agent carries, with their steps |
| `applications_list` | 0 | The person's applications, with status and progress |
| `applications_start` | 1 | Starts an application on a form; returns the first step |
| `applications_next` | 0 | The next step to ask — field, label, kind, choices, required — and how many remain |
| `applications_answer` | 1 | Records one answer, checked against the form; refused answers come back with their problems |
| `applications_attach` | 1, model | Attaches a document handed to the call to a document step: type, size and pages checked; what the form asks to read is read by the model and held to the form's rules; once accepted, the document is kept with the application |
| `applications_step` | 1, model | Asks the person the next step itself — a card with choices, or an attach button — then records the answer exactly as `answer` or `attach` would |
| `applications_review` | 0 | The whole application, what is missing, and whether it is ready |
| `applications_submit` | 3 | Closes a ready application and gives it a reference |
| `applications_withdraw` | 1 | Closes a draft without submitting |

Records: `application` (form, title, status, progress, reference,
submitted at), `answer` (one per answered step: the step, the question,
the value as checked, whether it was skipped) and `attachment` (one per
attached document: the step, the file, its type, size and pages, and
what was read from it). Files: `document` (each document accepted, kept
with its application: PDF, PNG, JPEG, up to 25 MB).

## Forms

A form is a YAML file in `forms/` with an `id`, a `title`, an optional
`description`, and its `steps`. The steps are asked in order. Each step
has a `field`, a `label` (the question), a `kind`, an optional `help`,
and the checks its answer must pass. A step is required unless it says
`required: false`; an empty answer skips an optional step.

| kind | checks |
|---|---|
| `text` | `min_length`, `max_length`, `pattern` with a `pattern_hint` for the refusal |
| `number` | `min`, `max`; stored to the cent |
| `date` | written as YYYY-MM-DD or refused; `not_before: today`; `after: <earlier date step>` |
| `choice` | one of `choices` (2 to 8); an optional choice step offers Skip |
| `email` | an address |
| `file` | `accept` (types), `max_mb`, `max_pages`; `read` names what the model reads from it; `checks` hold what was read to rules |

The one document check today is `date_after`: a date the model read
(`read_field`) must be at least `months` after an earlier date step
(`after_field`); its `message` is the refusal. A form that fails
these rules is refused by name and fault when the agent is used, not
silently asked in a broken shape.

Two forms are carried as examples: a travel authorization with a
passport copy, and an equipment request. Add your own beside them.

## What is checked, and by whom

- **Answers** are checked in code. A date not written as a date is not
  a date; a number outside its bounds is refused; a choice must be one
  offered. Nothing is guessed.
- **Documents** are checked in code for type, size, pages and
  emptiness. Where the form says what to read, the chat's model reads
  it: a PDF by its text, a photo by its pixels (`call.model(pictures=…)`).
  A PDF with no text layer (a scan) is refused with what to attach
  instead: the model is shown pictures only (PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP).
  Each value read is marked **verified** when the document's text
  carries it, **assumed** when it does not (or the document is a
  photo), **missing** when the model found nothing. The form's rules
  are then applied to what was read, and a value that could not be read
  as a date fails the rule that needs it rather than passing by absence.
- **Submission** is the person's: level 3, waiting for approval unless
  the chat was trusted with it, and refused while anything required is
  missing.

## The reference pattern

`applications_step` is the whole intake in one function: it asks the
person the next question as a card of the right shape (choices as
buttons; an attach button for a document), records the answer, and
reports what came of it. One question per call, so a call is short and
a restart between questions loses nothing — the record already holds
every accepted answer. The assistant calls it until it says done, then
`review`, then `submit` on the person's word.

## Limits

- The forms are files in this agent; changing one is a new version.
- A photo is read by the model, not verified against text: everything
  read from a photo is assumed.
- Submission closes the record and gives it a reference; handing it to
  an external system is a further agent's job.

agent.name: Box
agent.description: Your Box, through the assistant. Find a file, see who can open it, hand a copy to another agent to read, file or share on your go-ahead, and hear about what changed.
agent.instructions: Use this agent to find, fetch, file, share or watch files in a Box account. Files and folders are addressed by item_id (Box's numeric id; the top folder is "0"); take it from a search, a folder listing or shared_with_me, never invent one. files_download brings a copy into the platform as a file another agent (Documents, Sheets) can read; as_pdf converts an Office file on the way. Uploading, creating a folder, moving, renaming, trashing, sharing and un-sharing change the user's Box and may pause for approval; ask before each. Delete moves to the Box trash — say so. sharing_link shares with the user's company unless they explicitly ask for anyone with the link; never choose open access on your own. People are email addresses: resolve a name first (from a mail thread, or ask). Before sharing, sharing_permissions shows who can already open the file. To act on what changes in the account, record a watch ONCE (changes_watch) and schedule changes_new every few minutes; each check hands on only what changed since the last, oldest first, and a watch covers the whole account — narrow by the rows' folder as the user's instruction says. Never record a second watch for the same request.

functions.description: Files and folders other people own and shared with the account (Box keeps them at its top level), most recently changed first, each with its owner as shared_by.

functions.name: Get File
functions.description: One file or folder's details, by item_id.

functions.name: Download File
functions.description: Bring a copy of a file into the platform, for another agent to read. as_pdf converts a Word, Excel or PowerPoint file to PDF on the way. Folders cannot be downloaded; files larger than the platform can carry are refused before they are fetched.

functions.name: Upload File
functions.description: Put a file of the chat (file_ref) into a Box folder, under its own name or name. If the folder already has a file of that name, the new one is renamed unless on_conflict is "replace" (a new version of the same file) or "fail". Changes the user's Box — only on their go-ahead.

functions.name: Create Folder
functions.description: A new folder under folder_path or folder_id. Only on the user's go-ahead.

functions.name: Move or Rename
functions.description: Rename an item (new_name), move it to another folder (to_folder_path or to_folder_id), or both. Only on the user's go-ahead.

functions.description: Move an item to the Box trash, from which the user can restore it; a folder goes with what is in it. Only on the user's go-ahead.

functions.description: Everyone who can open an item — the owner, people invited (collaborators), access inherited from a folder above, and the shared link with how far it reaches.

functions.name: Share With People
functions.description: Give named people access to an item, read (viewer) or write (editor); Box emails them. Only on the user's go-ahead.

functions.name: Share by Link
functions.description: Open an item's shared link to everyone in the user's company (the default) or, only when the user asks for it, anyone with the link — view, or edit for a file — and return it. Only on the user's go-ahead.

functions.name: Stop Sharing
functions.description: Remove one permission (from sharing_permissions) from an item: a collaborator, or the shared link. The owner's cannot be removed, nor access inherited from a folder above. Only on the user's go-ahead.

functions.name: Watch for Changes
functions.description: Start watching the whole Box account for changes to files and folders, from now. Record it once, then schedule changes_new.

functions.name: What Changed
functions.description: What changed since the last check, for every watch (or one, by watch_ref): one row per event about a file or folder — uploaded, created, moved, renamed, trashed, restored, shared — oldest first, each naming its watch and who did it. An event Box delivers twice is handed on once. Moves each watch forward; "more" says a later check continues. Safe to schedule: it reads and records only.

agents.readme:
# Box (`box`)

"Where is the Riverside lease, and who can open it?" — found by name or
content, with everyone who has access: the owner, the collaborators,
anyone reaching it through a folder above, and whether its shared link
opens to the company or to anyone. Ask for a copy and it comes into the
chat as a file, where Documents can read it. Ask to put a file in
Contracts and share it with Dana, and each step waits for your go-ahead.
Ask to hear when something is uploaded, and a scheduled check hands on
what was.

The Google Drive, OneDrive and Dropbox agents' twin over Box API 2.0:
the same functions and the same rules, plus a change watch.

## Functions

| Function | Level | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `account_status` | 0 | The connection, the company it belongs to, and how full the account is |
| `files_search` | 0 | Files matching a query, by name or content |
| `files_list` | 0 | What is in a folder, folders first, by path or id |
| `files_shared_with_me` | 0 | Files and folders others own and shared, with their owner |
| `files_get` | 0 | One item's details |
| `files_download` | 2 | A copy handed back as a file of the chat; Office files can come in as PDF |
| `files_upload` | 3 | A file of the chat into a Box folder; never a duplicate name unless told |
| `files_create_folder` | 3 | A new folder |
| `files_move` | 3 | Renames, moves, or both |
| `files_delete` | 3 | To the Box trash, from which it can be restored |
| `sharing_permissions` | 0 | Who can open an item, and how |
| `sharing_invite` | 3 | Makes named people collaborators, viewer or editor; Box emails them |
| `sharing_link` | 3 | The shared link, for the company or for anyone when asked |
| `sharing_revoke` | 3 | Removes one collaborator, or the link |
| `changes_watch` | 1 | Starts watching the account's changes, from now |
| `changes_new` | 1, schedulable | What changed since the last check, oldest first; moves the watch forward |

Records: `share` — every grant and revocation this agent made; `watch`
— Box's stream position, and the events most recently handed on.

## Rules it keeps

- **Nothing in the Box changes without a yes.** Upload, folder, move,
  rename, trash, share and un-share are all level 3.
- **Delete means the trash.** A folder goes with what is in it; nothing
  here deletes for good.
- **An upload does not make a second file of the same name.** Box
  refuses a taken name, so the agent checks first and uses "name 1.ext",
  or, when asked (`on_conflict: replace`), uploads a new version of the
  file that is there.
- **A link is for the company.** "Anyone with the link" is made only
  when the user asks for it in those words. A personal account has no
  company, so the agent asks rather than widening it on its own. Only a
  file's link can allow editing.
- **The owner's access, and access given on a folder above, are not
  revoked here.**
- **People are addresses.** A name is refused until it is resolved.
- **A file too large to carry is refused before it is fetched,** with
  its size named.

## Watching for changes

The assistant records one watch (`changes_watch`) and schedules
`changes_new` every few minutes. A check calls no model, so one that
finds nothing costs nothing. The watch holds Box's own stream
position for the `changes` stream and hands on the events about files
and folders — uploaded, created, moved, copied, renamed, trashed,
restored, a version made current, a link made, changed or removed, a
collaborator added or removed — oldest first, with who did it. Box
says it may deliver an event twice; the watch remembers the ids it
handed on and never repeats one. A full chunk sets `more`. A watch
covers the whole account; the rows' `folder` narrows it.

## Where it differs from the drive twins

Box addresses files and folders separately; a bare id is tried as a
file, then as a folder. Box has no "shared with me" list — what others
share with the account sits at its top level, so that is where the
agent looks, and names each item's owner. An invitation carries no
personal message. A PDF of an Office file is Box's own rendering, made
on first request; if Box is still making it, the agent says to try
again shortly.

## Setup

1. In the [Box Developer Console](https://app.box.com/developers/console),
   create a **Custom App** with **User Authentication (OAuth 2.0)**.
2. Under **Configuration → OAuth 2.0 Redirect URI**, add the redirect
   URI DecentAI shows under Settings → Connected apps.
3. Under **Application Scopes**, tick **Read all files and folders
   stored in Box** and **Write all files and folders stored in Box**
   (`root_readwrite`), and save.
4. Paste the client id and secret into DecentAI under
   **Settings → Connected apps** as provider `box`.

Then, per Box account, anyone: **Agents → Box → Credentials → Connect
account**, sign in, done. Box issues a new refresh token each time the
platform refreshes; the platform keeps the newest.

Leave `api_base_url` empty; it exists for the tests. A company Box may
require an administrator to authorize the app before anyone can connect.

## Limits

- Files up to 25 MB each way.
- Search returns files, not folders.
- Live Box behaviour is verified against a loopback stub of the API
  subset it uses; the first real connection is the first live run.

agent.name: Code
agent.description: Writes a Python program for what you ask and runs it once you allow it. You see the program first, with what it is for and everything it needs: the packages it installs, the sites it reaches, the tokens it uses and the files it reads. It gives back what the program printed and the files it made.
agent.instructions: Use this agent when the work needs a program and no other installed agent does it: a calculation over files, reshaping or merging data, a chart, a file conversion, calling a web API. Call program_run with the goal written in full: what to work out, from which files, and what to give back. Pass the files the person attached in files. The agent writes the program, the person sees it with what it needs, and it runs only when they allow it; do not ask them for permission yourself first. The result says how it ended. done: report what output says, and never state a number the output does not show. The files it made are handed to the person with your answer by the platform: name them, and never write a link or an address for one. declined: the person said no; tell them so and do not call again with the same request unless they ask. unanswered: nobody answered. failed: say what went wrong in the words of the result. When the result has earlier_failure, a program before the last one failed and that is why another was shown: say so, in its words. To change a program that already ran, call again with the earlier code in code and the change in goal. The program runs alone: it cannot ask the person anything, so put every detail it needs in the goal. It reaches only the sites the person opened for it, and nothing inside the network the platform runs in.

functions.name: Write And Run
functions.description: Write a Python program for the goal, put it before the person with what it needs, and run it when they allow it. files are the files the program reads, handed to the call; they are in its working folder under their own names. code is a program to start from, for changing one that ran before. A program that fails is corrected and put before the person again, up to three programs in all. Returns the outcome (done, failed, declined, unanswered), a summary, what the program printed, the files it made, and the program itself.

agents.readme:
# Code (`code_runner`)

Someone has a spreadsheet of orders and wants the total by month and a
chart of it. No agent does exactly that, and they do not write code.
They ask; they are shown the program that would do it and what it
needs; they allow it.

This agent writes a Python program for a goal and runs it when the
person allows it. It is for the work no other agent does: a calculation
over files, data reshaped or merged, a chart, a file converted, a web
API that has no agent of its own.

## What the person sees

Every program goes before them before it runs, whole, with what it is
for and what it needs:

| Shown | What it is |
|---|---|
| Purpose | What the program does, in words |
| Installs | The packages it needs |
| Reaches | The sites it connects to |
| Uses | The tokens it is handed, each with the site it is for |
| Reads | The files it was given |
| The code | The whole program |

A program that reaches sites, or installs packages, asks the platform
to open those sites for the call (`network.open`): the person sees the
code, its purpose and the sites, and a yes opens them. A program that
reaches nothing is put to them as a question in the chat that shows it
(Run it / Don't run it); one too long for a question (4,000 characters)
is sent back to be written shorter. No answer, or a no, and it does not
run.

What runs is what they allowed. A program that fails is corrected and
goes before them again — a changed program is a new program, and it
says it is a correction — up to three programs in one call.

In a chat that does not yet trust an agent to make files, the
platform's own approval of the call comes before it, as for any
function at level 2.

## What the program gets

What the person allowed, and nothing else:

- **Sites.** Opened for that one call and closed when it ends. A site
  that was not named is refused, and so is every address inside the
  network the platform runs in. HOSTS names sites by name: an address or
  a wildcard is sent back to the writer before anyone sees it.
- **Packages.** The package index (`pypi.org`, `files.pythonhosted.org`)
  is opened with the program's sites. The agent installs what it named
  into a folder in its home, with the `pip` of the sandbox's Python 3.12
  base, before the program starts. The same list is kept for the next
  program that names it.
- **Tokens.** Each is kept in the `tokens` secret, by the site it is
  for, and used again for that site. One not kept yet is asked of the
  person on its form. The program reads it from its environment. A token
  is always for one of the sites the program named, and its value is
  taken out of whatever the program printed before that is given back.
- **Files.** The files handed to the call are in the program's working
  folder under their own names. Every file the program makes there is
  handed back as one of the chat's files, up to ten.

The program runs as the agent does: a user of its own, its files
fenced, one way out. It has five minutes (`DECENTAI_CODE_RUN_SECONDS`
in its environment changes that), no terminal, and nobody to ask.

**Why the manifest declares the package index.** The runtime starts an
agent's process with no network at all when its manifest declares no
host, and then nothing `network.open` opens could be reached. The two
package hosts are declared so that the process has a way out; every
other site is opened per call.

## Function

| Function | Level | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `program_run` | 2 | Writes a program for the goal, puts it before the person, runs it when they allow it, and returns what it printed and the files it made |

| Input | |
|---|---|
| `goal` | What the program should do, in full: it cannot ask anything |
| `files` | The files it reads, handed to the call; ten at most |
| `code` | A program to start from, for changing one that ran before |

The result also carries the program's `purpose` and `code`, the
`packages` and `hosts` it named, how many programs were shown
(`programs_shown`), `earlier_failure` when a program before the last
one failed, and `not_returned`: files it made that were not handed
back (past the tenth, or too large).

| Outcome | |
|---|---|
| `done` | It ran: `output` is what it printed, `files` what it made |
| `declined` | The person did not allow the program, or did not give a token it needs |
| `unanswered` | Nobody answered |
| `failed` | No program could be written for the goal, or three in a row failed; `summary` says which |

## Tests

`tests/test_code_runner.py` runs the agent's program as the runtime
does: programs are really written to disk and really run, and packages
really installed by pip from a local folder of wheels. The chat's model
is scripted, and the person is a scripted answer to the question, to
`network.open` and to the token's form.

agent.name: Connection Check
agent.description: See what an agent can reach from where it runs. It declares one host, tries that one, one it never declared, an address inside the network and a way around the platform, and says which were reached and which were refused, and by what.
agent.instructions: Use this agent when the person wants to see whether agents are held to the hosts they declared. check_report runs the whole check and is the place to start; check_reach tries one address the person names. Report every row as the result gives it: outcome is reached, refused, unreachable or not_tried, and they are different things. refused means the platform stopped it, and reason says why in the platform's own words; unreachable means it was allowed and the host did not answer; not_tried means this agent would not try it. Never say an attempt was refused when its outcome is unreachable, and never guess a reason the result does not give. This agent declares example.com and nothing else, so example.com reached and everything else refused is what a held agent looks like: say so plainly, and say as plainly when the verdict is that nothing holds it. It sends nothing to the hosts it tries and reads nothing from them.

Each row says what was expected of a held agent and what happened; held says whether every row went as expected.

Says whether this agent declared it, what happened, and the platform's reason when it was refused.

# Connection Check (`connection_check`)

Someone installs DecentAI and reads that an agent reaches the hosts it
declared and nothing else. They ask this agent to show it: it tries
the one host it declared, one it never declared, an address inside the
network and a way around the platform, and says what happened to each.

No credential, no records, no packages. An attempt is a connection
opened and closed: nothing is sent to a host it tries, and nothing is
read from one.

## Functions

| Function | Level | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `check_report` | 0 | The whole check, five attempts. Each row says what was expected of an agent that is held and what happened; `held` says whether every row went as expected, and `verdict` says it in a sentence; `runs_as` names the user the program runs as, where the system has one. The rows are also shown in the chat as a table |
| `check_reach` | 0 | One host the person names: a name, a name and a port (`host:8443`), or a whole http or https address, of which the host and the port are used; the port is 443 when none is given (80 for an http address). Says whether this agent declared it, what happened, and the platform's reason when it was refused |

## What the check tries

| Attempt | Target | A held agent |
|---|---|---|
| The host this agent declared | `example.com` | reaches it |
| A host it did not declare | `www.wikipedia.org` | is refused |
| An address inside the network | `169.254.169.254` | is refused |
| Past the proxy: a connection made straight | `1.1.1.1:443` | is refused |
| Past the proxy: a name looked up | `example.com` | is refused |

## Four outcomes

| Outcome | Means |
|---|---|
| `reached` | the connection was opened |
| `refused` | the platform stopped it; `reason` is in the platform's own words |
| `unreachable` | it was allowed, and the host did not answer |
| `not_tried` | this agent would not try it |

## What it says where nothing holds an agent

On a developer's machine, and anywhere a program is not run in the
sandbox, it is pointed at no proxy and connects as any program does. The check says so: `through_the_proxy` is false and the verdict
is that nothing holds this agent to the host it declared. There it
does not try an address inside the network at all, since nothing would
have refused it.

Where the proxy is offered and nothing makes it the only way out, the
verdict is *partly held*: what was not declared is refused by the
proxy, and the connection made past it was not stopped.

## Through the sandbox's way out

In the sandbox a program's network holds one address, `127.0.0.1:3128`,
an HTTP proxy named in `HTTPS_PROXY`, which carries each connection to
the runtime's way out; that knows the program by where the connection
arrived, so no pass is sent. The check asks it for a tunnel (`CONNECT`)
and reports its answer: 200 is `reached`; a refusal comes at once, and
its reason is the first line of what follows the answer's head (the
platform's way out writes it there) or else the answer's own first
line; a host the way out opened and could not reach is closed on
without an answer, and is `unreachable`. A connection made straight,
and a name looked up, have nowhere to go in the sandbox: no other
address, no name lookups.

## Where it connects

`example.com`, and the whole of it. Everything else it tries is meant
to be refused.

agent.name: Documents
agent.description: Reads the PDFs, Word files and text you upload and answers with page references and quoted evidence: extract the fields you name, compare two versions, fill a Word template, produce a Word or PDF file.
agent.instructions: Use this agent when the user attached a document or wants one produced. Start with read_inspect to learn what a file is and which pages are readable; then read_text for the words (by page) or read_extract for named fields with quoted evidence. Quote what a document says with its page; a field extract.found=false means the document does not state it — say so, never fill it in. Unreadable (scanned) pages are listed by number: tell the user those pages could not be read. compare_versions is deterministic and shows the changed passages side by side; use it before describing what changed. To make a file, give produce_docx or produce_pdf the sections and tables as data (never retype figures from memory — take them from an extract or a stored result), and give the user the file_ref. produce_fill_template reports placeholders it could not fill; ask for those values rather than guessing.

agents.readme:
# Documents (`documents`)

A forty-page supplier contract arrives as a PDF. Ask what the notice
period is and the answer comes with the page and the sentence it was
read from. Ask what changed since the last version and the differences
are listed, not guessed.

Reads uploaded PDF, Word and text documents page by page, says which
pages could not be read, extracts named fields with a quoted passage
behind each, compares two versions deterministically, fills Word
templates, and produces Word and PDF files that are read back before
they are returned.

No external service and no credential. Files come in as platform
files — a person's upload in the chat, or something another agent
saved (the Mail, Gmail or Outlook agent's `search_save_attachment`) — by `file_ref`.

## Supported formats

| Kind | Read | Produced |
|---|---|---|
| PDF with a text layer | yes, per page | yes (`produce_pdf`) |
| Scanned PDF, image-only pages | no — those pages are listed as unreadable, never skipped silently | — |
| Word `.docx` | yes, paragraphs and tables, headings listed | yes (`produce_docx`, `produce_fill_template`) |
| Plain text, Markdown, CSV | yes, as one page | — |
| Legacy `.doc`, spreadsheets, images | no — reported as unsupported | — |

## Functions

| Function | Level | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `read_inspect` | 0 | Kind, page count, characters in all, readable and unreadable page numbers, Word headings |
| `read_text` | 0 | The text by page, from `from_page`, up to `max_chars` (20,000 by default); says where to continue |
| `read_extract` | 1, uses the chat's model | Named fields with the passage that states each and its page. A field the document does not state is `found: false`; a quote not found verbatim in the text is `verified: false`. Recorded |
| `compare_versions` | 0 | Added, removed and changed passages between two files with their pages, up to `max_changes` (60); passages with a `focus` word first, and counted |
| `produce_docx` | 2 | A Word file from a title and sections with paragraphs and tables; read back |
| `produce_pdf` | 2 | A PDF from the same data; read back and its page count reported |
| `produce_fill_template` | 2 | A Word template's `{{placeholders}}` filled from values; unfilled ones are listed, never invented |

Records: `extract` (what was read from which file) and `output` (every
file produced, by name). Files: `source`, or a file handed to the call,
in; a produced file goes back as the call's file.

## Evidence, not opinion

`read_extract` asks the chat's model for the value *and* the passage
that states it, then checks the passage against the document's text
itself. A field comes back in one of three states: found and verified
on a page; found but unverified, meaning the model's quote is not in
the text verbatim and the value should be checked; or not found,
meaning the document does not state it. The agent never fills in a
price, a date or a term the document lacks.

`compare_versions` is sequence matching over paragraphs. It reports
what changed and where; what the change *means* is the assistant's to
say, with the passages in front of it.

## Sample data

Sidra Office Supplies: the Riverside office lease and invoice
INV-1043 as PDFs, and the Harbourline proposal in two versions as
Markdown, in `samples/` (`samples.yaml`). `tests/make_sample_pdfs.py`
writes the two PDFs.

## Limits, and what is not verified

- Reading depends on a text layer. OCR is not part of this agent; a
  scanned page is reported as unreadable.
- Extraction quality depends on the chat's model; the verification
  step catches a misquote, not a misreading of a verified passage.
- Templates: a placeholder's replacement lands in the paragraph's
  first run, so character-level formatting inside that paragraph may
  be lost. Paragraph styles survive.
- PDFs are produced with core fonts; characters outside Latin-1 are
  replaced.
- Produced files are verified by reading them back with the same
  library that wrote them and, for PDFs, extracting text; rendered
  appearance is not inspected.
- The tests run the agent as its own program; every fixture file is
  produced by the agent itself or is a hand-written minimal PDF.

agent.name: Dropbox
agent.description: Your Dropbox, through the assistant. Find a file, see who can open it, hand a copy to another agent to read, file or share on your go-ahead, and hear about what changed in a folder.
agent.instructions: Use this agent to find, fetch, file, share or watch files in a Dropbox account. Files are addressed by item_id (Dropbox's "id:…"); take it from a search, a folder listing or shared_with_me, never invent one — a path the user gave ("/Contracts/lease.pdf") works too. files_download brings a copy into the platform as a file another agent (Documents, Sheets) can read; as_pdf renders a Word or PowerPoint file as PDF on the way. Uploading, creating a folder, moving, renaming, deleting, sharing and un-sharing change the user's Dropbox and may pause for approval; ask before each. Delete moves to Dropbox's deleted files, restorable for as long as the account's plan keeps them — say so. sharing_link shares with the user's Dropbox team unless they explicitly ask for anyone with the link; never choose anonymous on your own. People are email addresses: resolve a name first (from a mail thread, or ask). Before sharing, sharing_permissions shows who can already open the file. To act on what changes in a folder, record a watch ONCE (changes_watch) and schedule changes_new every few minutes; each check hands on only what changed since the last. Never record a second watch for the same request. A watch listed under "reset" started again from now: say that changes in between may have been missed.

examples.prompt: Find the Riverside lease in my Dropbox and save a copy for me to read.

examples.prompt: Who has access to the Q3 budget workbook in Dropbox?

examples.prompt: Put the file I just attached in Contracts and share it with dana@sidra.example, view only.

examples.prompt: Watch my Dropbox Invoices folder and, whenever a file arrives, save a copy and tell me what it is.

functions.description: Files other people shared with the account, newest share first, with who shared each.

functions.name: Get File
functions.description: One file or folder's details, by item_id (or path).

functions.description: Bring a copy of a file into the platform, for another agent to read. as_pdf renders a Word or PowerPoint file as PDF on the way; a Dropbox Paper document comes in exported. Folders cannot be downloaded; files larger than the platform can carry are refused before they are fetched.

functions.name: Upload File
functions.description: Put a file of the chat (file_ref) into a Dropbox folder, under its own name or name. If the folder already has a file of that name, Dropbox gives the new one a numbered name unless on_conflict is "replace" (a new version of the same file) or "fail". Changes the user's Dropbox — only on their go-ahead.

functions.name: Create Folder
functions.description: A new folder under folder_path or folder_id. Only on the user's go-ahead.

functions.name: Move or Rename
functions.description: Rename an item (new_name), move it to another folder (to_folder_path or to_folder_id), or both. Only on the user's go-ahead.

functions.name: Delete
functions.description: Move an item to Dropbox's deleted files, from which the user can restore it for as long as their plan keeps deleted files. Only on the user's go-ahead.

functions.name: Who Has Access
functions.description: Everyone who can open an item — the owner, people and groups invited, access inherited from a shared parent folder, and each link with how far it reaches.

functions.name: Share With People
functions.description: Give named people access to an item, read or write; Dropbox emails them. A folder becomes a shared folder first. Only on the user's go-ahead.

functions.name: Share by Link
functions.description: A link to an item for the user's Dropbox team (the default) or, only when the user asks for it, anyone with the link — view or edit — and return it. An item that already has a link gets that link changed instead. Only on the user's go-ahead.

functions.name: Stop Sharing
functions.description: Remove one permission (from sharing_permissions) from an item: a person, a group, or a link. The owner's cannot be removed, nor access inherited from a shared parent folder. Only on the user's go-ahead.

functions.name: Watch a Folder
functions.description: Start watching a folder and everything under it, by folder_path or folder_id (the whole Dropbox by default), from now. Record it once, then schedule changes_new.

functions.name: What Changed
functions.description: What changed since the last check, for every watch (or one, by watch_ref): one row per file added or changed, and per item deleted, oldest first, each naming its watch. Moves each watch forward; "more" says a later check continues; "reset" lists watches Dropbox restarted from now. Safe to schedule: it reads and records only.

agents.readme:
# Dropbox (`dropbox`)

"Where is the Riverside lease, and who can open it?" — found by name or
content, with everyone who has access: the owner, the people invited,
anyone reaching it through a shared folder, and every link and how far
it reaches. Ask for a copy and it comes into the chat as a file, where
Documents can read it. Ask to put a file in Contracts and share it with
Dana, and each step waits for your go-ahead. Ask to hear when invoices
land in a folder, and a scheduled check hands on the ones that did.

The Google Drive and OneDrive agents' twin over Dropbox API v2: the same
functions and the same rules, plus a change watch.

## Functions

| Function | Level | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `account_status` | 0 | The connection, the team it belongs to, and how full the account is |
| `files_search` | 0 | Files and folders matching a query, by name or content |
| `files_list` | 0 | What is in a folder, folders first, by path or id |
| `files_shared_with_me` | 0 | Files others shared, newest share first, with who shared them |
| `files_get` | 0 | One item's details |
| `files_download` | 2 | A copy handed back as a file of the chat; Word and PowerPoint can come in as PDF |
| `files_upload` | 3 | A file of the chat into a Dropbox folder; never overwrites unless told |
| `files_create_folder` | 3 | A new folder |
| `files_move` | 3 | Renames, moves, or both |
| `files_delete` | 3 | To Dropbox's deleted files, from which it can be restored |
| `sharing_permissions` | 0 | Who can open an item, and how |
| `sharing_invite` | 3 | Gives named people read or write access, with an optional message; Dropbox emails them. A folder becomes a shared folder first |
| `sharing_link` | 3 | A link for the team, or for anyone when asked |
| `sharing_revoke` | 3 | Removes one person, group or link |
| `changes_watch` | 1 | Starts watching a folder and everything under it, from now |
| `changes_new` | 1, schedulable | What changed since the last check; moves the watch forward |

Records: `share` — every grant and revocation this agent made; `watch`
— the folders watched, and Dropbox's cursor for each.

## Rules it keeps

- **Nothing in the Dropbox changes without a yes.** Upload, folder,
  move, rename, delete, share and un-share are all level 3.
- **Delete means Dropbox's deleted files.** They can be restored for as
  long as the account's plan keeps them; nothing here deletes for good.
- **An upload never overwrites by default.** A name already taken gets
  Dropbox's own numbered name ("name (1).ext"); replacing is asked for
  by name (`on_conflict: replace`), and Dropbox keeps the old version.
- **A link is for the team.** "Anyone with the link" is made only when
  the user asks for it in those words. A personal account has no team,
  so the agent asks rather than widening it on its own. An item that
  already has a link gets that link changed, not a second one.
- **The owner's access, and access that comes from a shared parent
  folder, are not revoked here.**
- **People are addresses.** A name is refused until it is resolved.
- **A file too large to carry is refused before it is fetched,** with
  its size named.

## Watching a folder

The assistant records one watch (`changes_watch`) and schedules
`changes_new` every few minutes. A check calls no model, so one that
finds nothing costs nothing. The watch holds Dropbox's own
`list_folder` cursor, so each change is handed on once: files added or
changed (Dropbox does not say which), and anything deleted, with who
changed a file when it sits in a shared folder. Dropbox pages changes
25 at a time; `more` says the next check continues. If Dropbox declares
the cursor stale, the watch starts again from now and is listed under
`reset` — whatever changed in between was not seen.

## Where it differs from the drive twins

Dropbox has real paths, so every function takes a path ("/Contracts/
lease.pdf") as well as an id ("id:…"), and each row carries both. A
Word or PowerPoint file converts to PDF through Dropbox's preview;
spreadsheets do not (Dropbox previews them as HTML). A Dropbox Paper
document has no bytes of its own and comes in exported. A file shared
with the account but never added to it is fetched through its link.
Dropbox keeps no web address for an item, so `link` is filled only
where Dropbox gave one.

## Setup

1. In the [Dropbox App Console](https://www.dropbox.com/developers/apps),
   create an app with **Scoped access** and **Full Dropbox** access.
2. Under **Permissions**, tick `account_info.read`,
   `files.metadata.read`, `files.content.read`, `files.content.write`,
   `sharing.read` and `sharing.write`, and submit.
3. Under **Settings → OAuth 2 → Redirect URIs**, add the redirect URI
   DecentAI shows under Settings → Connected apps.
4. Paste the app key and app secret into DecentAI under
   **Settings → Connected apps** as provider `dropbox` (client id and
   client secret).

Then, per Dropbox account, anyone: **Agents → Dropbox → Credentials →
Connect account**, sign in, done. The platform asks Dropbox for offline
access, so the connection keeps refreshing.

Leave `api_base_url` empty; it exists for the tests.

## Limits

- Files up to 25 MB each way.
- The account's own Dropbox and files shared with it; team spaces are
  browsed only as far as they appear in the account's Dropbox.
- A new app works for its developer and up to 500 users before Dropbox's
  production review.
- Live Dropbox behaviour is verified against a loopback stub of the API
  subset it uses; the first real connection is the first live run.

agent.name: Excel Online
agent.description: Excel workbooks in your Microsoft 365 OneDrive, through the assistant. Find a workbook, read a sheet or a table, add rows or change cells on your go-ahead, and have a scheduled check hand on only the rows that arrived.
agent.instructions: Use this agent to read or change Excel workbooks (.xlsx) in the user's OneDrive. Find the workbook first (workbooks_find) and take its workbook_id from the result; never invent an id, a worksheet name or a table name — workbooks_get lists the worksheets and tables a workbook really has. Prefer a table when there is one: table_rows reads rows keyed by header, and table_add_rows appends rows given as objects keyed by those same headers. range_read reads a block by A1 address (A1:D40), or the used range when no address is given; say when rows_cut or columns_cut shows the answer was capped. table_add_rows and range_update change the user's workbook, may pause for approval, and are each recorded; range_update keeps what the cells held before, so show the user what will be replaced before asking. A write that comes back "unknown" may have landed: read the table or range before trying again. To act on rows as they are added, record a watch ONCE (rows_watch, on a table when the workbook has one, otherwise a worksheet) and schedule rows_new; each check returns only the rows added since the last one, keyed by header and naming its watch. A watch listed in "reset" lost rows since the last check and reported nothing this time — tell the user in one sentence. Never record a second watch for the same request.

examples.prompt: Open the Sidra orders workbook in my OneDrive and show me the last ten rows of the Orders table.

examples.title: Add a row
examples.prompt: Add a row to the Orders table: Harbourline, 20 desks, AED 18,400, due 30 November.

examples.title: Watch for new rows
examples.prompt: Watch the Orders table and, whenever a new order is added, tell me the customer and the amount.

secrets.label: Microsoft Account
secrets.description: A Microsoft 365 account, connected by signing in — the same connection the other Microsoft agents use; grant one saved account to all of them. The platform keeps and refreshes the tokens; this agent receives a short-lived access token. api_base_url is for tests only; leave it empty.

data.label: Workbook Write
data.description: Every change this agent made to a workbook: rows appended to a table, or a range overwritten with what it held before.

data.label: Row Watch
data.description: A table or worksheet the user wants to hear about as rows are added, and how many data rows it held at the last check.

functions.name: Account Status
functions.description: Confirm the Microsoft connection works and which address it is.

functions.name: Find Workbooks
functions.description: Excel workbooks (.xlsx only) whose name or content matches query, anywhere in the drive; every workbook when query is left out. Each row carries the workbook_id the other functions take.

functions.name: Inside A Workbook
functions.description: A workbook's worksheets (each with the block of cells in use and its row and column counts) and tables (each with its worksheet, header row and number of data rows).

functions.name: Read Range
functions.description: The cells of a worksheet block, by A1 address ("A1:D40", "B7"), or the worksheet's used range when address is left out, as rows of text as Excel shows it. header takes the first row as the header. At most max_rows rows and 50 columns come back; rows_cut and columns_cut say how many were left out.

functions.name: Overwrite Range
functions.description: Write values into a worksheet block given by A1 address; values must be exactly the block's rows and columns (a null leaves that cell as it is). What the cells held before is kept in the write record and returned. Changes the user's workbook — only on their go-ahead.

functions.name: Table Rows
functions.description: A table's data rows as objects keyed by its headers, in table order, a page at a time; next_page_token continues.

functions.name: Add Table Rows
functions.description: Append rows to the end of a table, each given as an object keyed by the table's headers (a header left out stays empty; a name the table does not have is refused). Lands as one change and is recorded. Changes the user's workbook — only on their go-ahead.

functions.name: Watch For New Rows
functions.description: Start watching a table (preferred) or a worksheet's used range for rows added from now on. Record it once, then schedule rows_new.

functions.name: New Rows
functions.description: The rows added since the last check, for every row watch (or one, by watch_ref): oldest first, keyed by header, each naming its watch and worksheet row. Moves the watch forward; "more" says a later check continues. A watch whose table or sheet lost rows reports nothing, starts again from its current size and is listed in "reset" with a sentence. Safe to schedule: it runs unattended.

agents.readme:
# Excel Online (`excel_online`)

"What came into the Orders table this week, and add Harbourline's
twenty desks to it" — the workbook is found in OneDrive, the table read
by its headers, and the new row waits for your go-ahead before it is
written. Ask to be told when an order is added, and a scheduled check
hands on only the orders that were.

Excel workbooks (.xlsx) in one Microsoft 365 OneDrive, read and written
where they are, over Microsoft Graph's workbook API. Nothing is
downloaded: only the cells asked for cross into the platform. It rides
the same Microsoft connection as the other Microsoft agents: connect
once, grant the one saved account to each.

## Functions

| Function | Level | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `account_status` | 0 | The connection, and which address it is |
| `workbooks_find` | 0 | .xlsx workbooks matching a query (every workbook when none is given) |
| `workbooks_get` | 0 | A workbook's worksheets (used range, rows, columns) and tables (worksheet, header row, row count) |
| `range_read` | 0 | A block by A1 address, or the used range, as rows of text; `header` takes the first row as the header; says how many rows and columns were cut |
| `table_rows` | 0 | A table's rows as objects keyed by header, a page at a time |
| `table_add_rows` | 3 | Appends rows given as objects keyed by header, in one workbook session; recorded |
| `range_update` | 3 | Overwrites a block, in one workbook session; recorded with what the cells held before |
| `rows_watch` | 1 | Starts watching a table (preferred) or a worksheet for rows added from now |
| `rows_new` | 1, schedulable | Rows added since the last check, keyed by header, each naming its watch; moves the watch; `more`; `reset` |

Records: `write` — every append and overwrite this agent made, with
what it wrote and, for an overwrite, the previous cells as formulas
(what would put them back); a write whose answer never came is
`unknown`. `watch` — each watched table or worksheet and how many data
rows it held at the last check.

## Watching for new rows

The assistant records one watch and schedules `rows_new` every few
minutes. A check needs no model; the rows it returns are those added
since the last one,
and the standing instruction in that chat says what to do with each.

The watch is a row count: rows past it are new, because a table grows
at the end. When the count has shrunk — rows deleted, or a sort pasted
over — the rows past the old count cannot be told apart from rows that
moved, so nothing is reported for that watch that time, the count
starts again from the table's current size, and `reset` names the
watch with a sentence the assistant can pass on. A table's rows are
preferred to a worksheet's used range: a table knows its own header
and end, while a used range also grows when someone types a note two
rows below the data.

## Rules it keeps

- **Nothing in a workbook changes without a yes.** Appending and
  overwriting are level 3.
- **A column is a header, not a letter.** Rows to append are keyed by
  header; a name the table lacks is refused, never dropped.
- **An overwrite keeps the old cells.** The shape must match the
  address exactly (25 rows and 20 columns at most; a null leaves its
  cell as it is), and the previous content is recorded and returned
  before anyone has to ask.
- **Reads are capped.** At most 25 rows per read and 50 columns, each
  cell's text cut at 300 characters, with the count of the rows and
  columns left out (`rows_cut`, `columns_cut`). Appends take 25 rows
  at a time.
- **Cells are read as text** — the date and the amount as Excel shows
  them — rather than as serial numbers and bare floats.

## Setup

The Microsoft connection is the one the other Microsoft agents use: an
app registration in Microsoft Entra with the delegated Graph
permissions listed in the manifest (`Files.ReadWrite.All` is the one
this agent needs), pasted into **Settings → Connected apps** as
provider `microsoft`. Then **Agents → Excel Online → Credentials →
Connect account**, or grant an account already connected for another
Microsoft agent. The `api_base_url` field exists so the tests can point
the agent at a loopback stub; leave it empty.

## Limits, and what is not verified

- Only .xlsx workbooks in the account's own OneDrive. Workbooks in
  SharePoint libraries or shared from someone else's drive are not
  addressed; .xls, .xlsm and .csv are not opened by the workbook API.
- A row watch sees rows added at the end. Rows inserted in the middle
  or edited in place are not new rows.
- The tests run the agent's program against a loopback stub of
  the Graph subset it uses (`tests/graph_workbook_stub.py`); the first
  real connection is the first live run. Details taken from Microsoft's
  documentation and not yet confirmed live:
  - that `$select=text` / `$select=formulas` is honoured on
    `worksheets/{name}/range(address='…')`, and `$select=address` on a
    table's `range`;
  - that `usedRange(valuesOnly=true)` answers "A1" for an empty sheet;
  - that a table with no data rows reports one blank body row, which
    is counted here as zero rows;
  - that `createSession` with `persistChanges: true`, the
    `workbook-session-id` header on `rows/add` and on a range `PATCH`,
    and `closeSession` behave as documented on a personal (consumer)
    OneDrive as well as a business one;
  - that drive search with the query `xlsx` finds workbooks by
    extension when no query is given.

agents.readme:
# Expenses (`expenses`)

A week of travel leaves eleven receipts as PDFs. Upload them and ask for
a claim: each line shows the receipt text it came from, the two taxi
receipts that are the same ride are flagged, and the hotel line that
breaks the policy says which rule. Submit it, and the approver's
decision is recorded under their name.

Receipts into an expense claim, with every extracted fact checked
against the receipt's own text, assumptions kept apart from facts,
duplicates matched in code, the company policy as rules with quoted
sources, and a claim status that becomes approved or paid only on a
named reviewer's word.

No external service and no credential.

## Functions

| Function | Level | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `claims_list` | 0 | The person's claims with their refs — how an existing claim is found |
| `claims_create` | 1 | A draft claim for a claimant, USD unless said otherwise |
| `claims_get` | 0 | The claim, its receipts, totals by currency, how many need attention |
| `claims_check` | 1 | Duplicates, receipts needing review or entry, other currencies, policy exceptions |
| `claims_workbook` | 2 | Receipts, Summary, Exceptions, Rules applied — read back, and handed back as the call's file |
| `claims_set_status` | 1 | draft → submitted on the claimant's word; approved, rejected, paid only with the reviewer's name |
| `receipts_read` | 1, uses the chat's model | One receipt file (PDF, text or photo) into a draft claim: merchant, date, currency, amount, category — verified or assumed |
| `receipts_confirm` | 1 | A person confirms or corrects a receipt; required for photos and anything needing review |
| `policies_load` | 1, uses the chat's model | The known rules out of the policy document, each with its sentence, checked verbatim |
| `policies_set_rule` | 1 | One rule set or corrected by a person |
| `policies_get` | 0 | The rules in force |

Records: `claim`, `receipt`, `rule` (rules are editable on the page).
Files: `receipt_file`, `policy_file` (or a file handed to the call); the
workbook goes back as the call's file.

## Facts and assumptions

`receipts_read` asks the chat's model for the fields and then checks:

- the **amount** must appear on the receipt as a money figure, or it
  is assumed; if a larger figure is printed, the note says so;
- the **date** must parse — ISO, written with a month name, or
  day/month/year when the order is unambiguous — or it is assumed;
- the **currency** must be shown on the receipt by code or symbol, or
  it is assumed; a receipt showing exactly one currency is taken as
  that currency;
- the **merchant** must appear in the text, or it is assumed;
- the **category** is always the model's judgement and is listed as
  assumed.

A receipt with any assumed money fact is `needs_review` and cannot be
in a submitted claim until a person confirms it. A photo (jpeg, png)
or a scanned PDF has no text this agent can read: it is recorded as
`manual` with the file kept, for `receipts_confirm` to fill.

Another currency is claimed as it is and flagged; nothing is
converted.

## Duplicates and policy

A duplicate is the same merchant, date and amount already recorded —
in this claim or any other. It is flagged on read and again by
`claims_check`, which marks it `duplicate`.

`policies_load` reads six rule names out of the policy document —
meal allowance per day, hotel per night, taxi per trip, receipt
required above, claim window in days, alcohol allowed — each with the
sentence that states it, verified against the text. A rule the policy
does not state is reported as not found and never assumed; a person
can set it with `policies_set_rule`. `claims_check` applies the meal
allowance (per day, in the claim's currency), hotel per night (to
accommodation lines), taxi per trip (to transport lines) and the claim
window (against `as_of`, today by default), and names each exception
with its figures. `receipt_required_above` and `alcohol_allowed` are
listed under the rules applied but raise no exception.

## Status

Preparing a claim proves nothing about reimbursement. `set_status`
lets the claimant submit a claim that has receipts and none still
needing review or entry; approved, rejected and paid require the
reviewer's name and are stamped with the date. The agent never reports a claim as
approved or paid on its own account.

## Sample data

Sidra Office Supplies: Sami's Dubai trip, a claim in draft with four
text receipts (a hotel night, a dinner over the meal allowance, and the
same taxi ride twice), and the travel policy in `samples/` with its six
rules already loaded (`samples.yaml`).

## Limits

- No OCR and no image reading; photos are manual entry.
- Dates with ambiguous day/month order (03/04/2026) are not read.
- Meal allowance is checked per calendar day in the claim's currency;
  other currencies are flagged, not summed against the allowance.
- Rules are one value each; tiered or per-city allowances are not
  modelled.

To follow feeds on a cadence, schedule feeds_new_items: it returns new items across subscriptions (or one), oldest first, each naming its feed, and "more" when a later check continues. "failed" lists feeds that could not be fetched and how many times in a row; mention them, but they are not news. feeds_read shows a feed's latest items without subscribing. agents.readme:
# Feeds (`feeds`)

A book fair's news page, a software vendor's release notes, a status
page. Subscribe once with the site's address and every morning the
assistant hears what was published since yesterday — each item once,
and nothing on a quiet day.

Follows RSS and Atom feeds: subscribes to a feed URL or to the feed a
web page advertises, reads a feed without subscribing, and hands on the
items published since the last check. Each subscription is a record
holding its cursor.

No credential.

## Functions

| Function | Level | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `feeds_add` | 1 | Subscribes to a feed URL, or discovers the feed from a web page's `<link rel="alternate" type="application/rss+xml">` (or `atom+xml`, `rdf+xml`). Starts from now: what the feed already holds is not news. Subscribing to the same feed again returns the existing subscription |
| `feeds_list` | 0 | The subscriptions (25, with the total): how far each was read, consecutive failures |
| `feeds_remove` | 1 | Deletes a subscription |
| `feeds_read` | 0 | The latest items of a feed or a page's feed without subscribing (`max_results`, 10 by default, 25 at most), in the feed's order, with the total: title, link, published (UTC), a plain-text summary clipped to 300 characters, author |
| `feeds_new_items` | 1, schedulable | New items across subscriptions (or one), oldest first, each naming its feed; moves each cursor through what it returned; `more` when a later check continues. Failures go in `failed` |

Records: `feed`.

## Formats

RSS 2.0, RSS 1.0 (RDF) and Atom 1.0, read with the standard library's
XML parser. Namespaces are ignored, so Dublin Core `dc:date` and
`dc:creator` are read in any of them. Dates in RFC 822 (`Wed, 09 Sep
2026 10:00:00 +0400`) and ISO 8601 (`2026-09-10T08:30:00+02:00`,
`2026-09-01`) are converted to UTC; a date that cannot be read leaves
the item undated rather than guessed. An item's id is its `guid` or
Atom `id`, else its link, else a digest of its title and summary.

A feed that declares XML entities is refused unparsed.

## The cursor, and exactly once

A subscription keeps:

- `cursor_time` — the newest published (or updated) time handed on;
- `cursor_ids` — the ids at exactly that time, so a second item in the
  same second is neither lost nor shown twice;
- `seen_ids` — the latest ids seen (up to 50, within one record field).

An item is new when its id is not in `seen_ids` and it is either later
than the cursor, or at the cursor's time with an id not yet handed on.
**An item without a date counts as new only if its id is not in the
seen list**, and only among the first 50 items of its feed, so a long
undated feed cannot flood the first check.

`feeds_new_items` gathers what is new in every feed, sorts it oldest first,
returns at most `max_results` (20 by default, 25 at most) and moves each feed's cursor
only through the items it returned; the rest are next time's, and
`more` says so.

Schedule it to follow feeds on a cadence. A feed that cannot be fetched
or parsed is listed in `failed` and counted on its record (`failures`,
`last_error`); it is not news. A
run checks at most 25 feeds, least recently checked first, and stops
starting new fetches after four minutes.

## Safety: only public addresses

Every fetch — the page, the discovered feed, and each redirect hop —
refuses loopback, private, link-local, multicast, reserved and
unspecified addresses (IPv4 and IPv6), checks the connected address as
well as the resolved one, follows at most 5 redirects, reads at most
5 MB with 10 s connect / 20 s read timeouts and 45 s in all, ignores
environment proxies (all but the sandbox's way out, `HTTPS_PROXY`), and
names itself `DecentAI-Feeds/0.1`. A page that advertises a
feed on a private address is refused like any other private address.
See [`web_reader/README.md`](../web_reader/README.md) for the details; this agent carries the same
`tools/fetch.py`.

**Test-only:** `DECENTAI_WEB_ALLOW_LOOPBACK=1` permits loopback and
nothing else, for the tests' loopback server. Never set it in a
deployment.

## Limits, and what is not verified

- A feed whose items change their `guid` on every fetch reports them
  again; a feed that re-dates an old item to a later time without a
  stable id may too.
- Seen ids are bounded (50). An undated item that drops out of that
  list while still near the top of its feed could be reported again;
  dated items are protected by the cursor.
- Only the first feed a page advertises is used; give the feed URL to
  choose another.
- A feed larger than 5 MB is refused, not read in part. Only the first
  500 items of a feed are read.
- Summaries are plain text clipped to 300 characters; follow the link
  (Web Reader) for the rest.
- Tested against a loopback server with hand-written RSS, Atom and RDF
  documents; real feeds have not been exercised.

agent.name: Gmail
agent.description: Your Gmail, read and answered through the assistant. Find a conversation, read it whole, draft the reply and see it before anything is sent; sending is a separate step you approve; a watch reminds you only while a reply is still missing; and an inbox watch reports only the mail that arrived since its last check.
agent.instructions: Use this agent when the user wants to find, read, answer or follow up on email. A person may have more than one account connected: account_list names them, and every function that reads or writes mail takes an optional account (the address) — pass it when the user names an inbox or when the agent says several are connected; a draft, a watch and an inbox watch remember the account they were made on. Always find the thread first (search_find, then search_thread) and quote what it actually says; never invent a message, a sender, a date or an id. A reply or a new message is prepared as a DRAFT (draft_reply / draft_compose) and shown to the user before anything is sent; draft_send is a separate external action that needs the user's explicit go-ahead and may pause for approval. A send that comes back "unknown" was not confirmed by Gmail — say so and do not send again; the user should check the Sent folder. To be reminded when a thread has not been answered, record a watch (watch_await_reply) and schedule watch_check; its "unanswered" list is empty once every reply came. To act on mail as it arrives, record an inbox watch ONCE (watch_inbox — narrow it with only_from / skip_from when the user names senders) and schedule watch_new_mail every few minutes; each run's "messages" holds only what arrived since the last check, with its thread_id, so read the thread and act on it as the user's standing instruction says. Never record a second inbox watch for the same request. Gmail search syntax works in query (from:, subject:, newer_than:7d, has:attachment). Message and thread ids and links are Gmail's own — pass them on unchanged.

agents.readme:
# Gmail (`gmail`)

Dana at Harbourline asks for a quotation for twenty desks. Ask the
assistant to find her email, draft the reply, and remind you on Thursday
if she has not answered. The draft appears in Gmail before it goes
anywhere; the send needs your go-ahead; and Thursday's reminder fires
only if the thread is still quiet.

Finds and reads Gmail conversations, prepares replies and new messages
as Gmail drafts, sends a draft only on explicit authorization, saves
attachments as files for other agents, watches a thread for a reply
so a schedule can remind the user only while the reply is still
missing, and watches the inbox so a schedule hands on only the mail
that arrived since its last check.

One Google account per credential, connected by signing in: the
platform runs the consent, keeps the refresh token and refreshes it;
the agent receives a short-lived access token and the address. A
person may connect more than one: `account_list` names them, every
function that reads or writes mail takes an optional `account` (the
address, or part of it), and a draft, a watch and an inbox watch
remember the account they were made on. With none named, the one
account kept answers; with several, the agent says which are connected
and asks for one. With none, the person is asked to connect one
(`account_status` only reports it).

## Functions

| Function | Level | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `account_status` | 0 | Confirms the connection and which address it is |
| `account_list` | 0 | The connected accounts by address |
| `search_find` | 0 | Gmail query syntax → one row per message, newest first, with `thread_id` and a link; `page_token` continues |
| `search_thread` | 0 | One conversation whole: senders, dates, body text (cut at `max_body_chars`), attachment list with ids |
| `search_save_attachment` | 2 | One attachment handed to the chat as a file (`file_ref`) for Documents or Spreadsheets to read |
| `draft_reply` | 1 | A reply prepared as a Gmail draft in the thread, to the last sender unless `to` is given (when the last message is the account's own, to its recipients); optional `cc`. Nothing is sent |
| `draft_compose` | 1 | A new message prepared as a Gmail draft: `to`, `subject`, `body`, optional `cc`. Nothing is sent |
| `draft_send` | 3 | Sends a prepared draft. Succeeds only when Gmail returns the sent message's id |
| `draft_discard` | 1 | Deletes the Gmail draft and marks the record discarded |
| `watch_await_reply` | 1 | Records that the user waits for a reply on a thread, from now |
| `watch_check` | 1, schedulable | Checks waiting watches; `unanswered` lists threads still without a reply from anyone else |
| `watch_inbox` | 1 | Starts watching the inbox from now (or from `since`; a `since` in the future by the mailbox's UTC clock is taken as now, and the result's `note` says so); `only_from` / `skip_from` name the senders that count, as addresses or `@domain`s |
| `watch_new_mail` | 1, schedulable | What arrived since the last check, oldest first, one row per message naming its watch; moves the watch forward; `more` says a later check continues |

Records: `draft` (what was prepared and what became of it), `watch`
(threads awaited) and `inbox` (how far the inbox has been read).

## Watching the inbox

The assistant records one inbox watch and schedules `watch_new_mail`
every few minutes. A check that finds nothing reports an empty
`messages`; a check that finds mail reports the rows, and the standing
instruction in that chat says what to do with each. The watch is a timestamp cursor in Gmail's
own clock — the time of the newest message handed on, plus the ids
that sit exactly on that second — so a second mail in the same second
is neither lost nor shown twice. Gmail lists newest first and cannot be
asked for oldest first, so a check walks the ids that arrived since
the cursor and reads the oldest of them; a burst larger than
`max_results` is handed on across checks, never skipped. Mail from the
account itself never counts; `only_from` and `skip_from` keep a
newsletter out. The cursor moves when the rows are handed on, so rows
the assistant failed to act on are not offered again.

## The reminder pattern

"Remind me tomorrow if they haven't replied":

1. `watch_await_reply {thread_id}` → `watch_ref`.
2. The assistant schedules `watch_check` for tomorrow, optionally with
   `inputs: {watch_ref}`.
3. The schedule runs it with no model. If the reply came, `unanswered`
   is empty. If not, it lists the thread and the note, and the
   assistant decides what to do.

## Send outcomes

`draft_send` has three outcomes and words them differently:

- **sent** — Gmail returned the sent message's id; recorded on the draft.
- **error** — Gmail refused; the draft stays `prepared` and may be
  sent again once the cause is fixed.
- **unknown** — the request was made and no answer came back. The draft
  is marked `unknown` and this function will not send it again; the
  user should look in the Sent folder. Reads are retried once on a
  dropped connection; writes never are.

A grant the provider no longer accepts is reported as `kind: auth`
with the instruction to reconnect. Every message and thread id, and
every link, is Gmail's own.

## Setup

Once per organization, by an administrator, in the Google Cloud console:

1. Enable the APIs the Google agents call under APIs & Services →
   Library: **Gmail**, **Google Calendar**, **Google Drive**, **Google
   Sheets**, **Google Docs**, **Google Forms** and **Google Tasks**.
2. OAuth consent screen: type External, the scopes every Google agent
   in the catalog shares — `openid`, `userinfo.email`, `gmail.modify`,
   `calendar`, `drive`, `spreadsheets`, `documents`,
   `forms.body.readonly`, `forms.responses.readonly` and `tasks` — your
   accounts as test users, then **publish** it. A consent screen left in Testing
   expires refresh tokens after seven days.
3. Credentials → OAuth client ID → **Web application**, with the
   redirect URI DecentAI shows under Settings → Connected apps.
4. Paste the client id and secret into DecentAI under
   **Settings → Connected apps** as provider `google`.

Then, per Google account, anyone: **Agents → Gmail → Credentials →
Connect account**, sign in, done. The credential is named after the
address and can be granted to every other Google agent as well. An
account connected before the shared list grew needs one reconnect. The
`api_base_url` field exists so the tests can point the agent at a
loopback stub; leave it empty.

## Limits, and what is not verified

- Live Gmail behaviour is **not yet verified**: the tests run the agent
  as its own program against a loopback stub of the Gmail API subset it
  uses. Live verification is pending a real account's token.
- `search_find` makes one metadata call per row (Gmail's list returns
  ids only); `max_results` is capped at 25 per page for that reason.
- Bodies prefer `text/plain`; HTML-only messages are stripped to text.
- Saved attachments must fit the platform's 25 MB; a larger one is
  refused with its size (`kind: too_large`).
- The agent never sends without `draft_send`, and `draft_send` never
  retries an unknown outcome.
- Photos and inline images are not read; they are listed as
  attachments and can be saved.
